newsitem.title: QATAR: Oil prices to remain weak to 2000 - IEA's Priddle.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices to remain weak to 2000 - IEA's Priddle.

text.p: Oil prices will remain weak through the next three to four years because of ample supplies, IEA executive director Robert Priddle said on Wednesday.
"Nobody should read too much into the recent increases...it could be mere snapshot rather than a trend," Priddle told Reuters in an interview on the sidelines of an energy experts meeting here.
Oil prices last year passed $25 a barrel -- $4 more than OPEC's target -- but slid to $17 earlier this year before picking up in the past few days.
"But this may be just transitional...there is ample supply in the market," Priddle said. He declined to forecast prices.
Priddle said a lot of excess oil was entering the market from non-OPEC producers set to increase their output to 47 million barrels per day (bpd) in the next few years from 42 million bpd.
But through the year 2010 OPEC members, especially Gulf Arab producers, would be the real winners when demand rises to 95 million bpd from 70 million now.
OPEC's six Gulf members -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar, Iran and Iraq -- control 65 percent of the world's total crude oil reserves and 30 percent of the world's gas.

Abdullah bin Salem al-Khulaifi, a leading Gulf Cooperation Council official, stressed the need for assurances "in the form of demand management guarantees" from oil consuming countries to help GCC states to develop reserves and build sufficient production capacity to meet future demand.
The GCC groups Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Oman, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar.

"Although we in the GCC are committed to maintain the security of supplies, oil and gas reserves are not automatically translated into production capacity," said Khulaifi, GCC deputy secretary-general for economic affairs.
"According to a study by OPEC's secretariat, the investment cost of raising sustainable production capacity by 10 million bpd is around $160 billion", he told the meeting.
"The call on OPEC is projected to rise from 28 million bpd at present to nearly 50 million bpd in 2010 -- over half of world oil requirements", he said.
"Apart from Venezuela, the only OPEC members with an ability to raise their production significantly are those in the Middle East, in particular the GCC countries," he added.

"With our massive reserves, which stand at around 46 percent of the world's total, we can sustain current levels of production for at least the next 90 years and are well-placed to raise output," said Khulaifi.
"While OECD countries presently account for 25 percent of world oil production, they possessed only six percent of world reserves," he said.
"With a reserve-to-production ratio of fewer than 10 years, output from the OECD is forecast (by IEA world energy outlook) to decline to around 15 percent of the world output by 2010".
Khulaifi said if GCC producers were to undertake further massive expansion programmes to meet future world demand they needed to secure markets for their products.
